prose:
Start with the math and the mechanics, not with a framework. You should be comfortable with matrix multiplication, gradients, and the idea that a weight update can be approximated as a low-rank product: instead of updating a full weight matrix W, you freeze W and learn ΔW = B·A, where A is r×d and B is d×r, scaled by alpha/r. Then learn PyTorch well enough to write a custom nn.Module, and get familiar with the Hugging Face Transformers model you plan to adapt (attention projections, MLP blocks, tokenizer, training loop). If you skip the “what does a forward/backward pass actually do” step, LoRA will feel like magic and your capstone will be a wrapper around PEFT rather than an implementation.

A sensible build path: first implement LoRA from scratch on a tiny model you can train on your laptop — e.g., a small GPT-style model or distilgpt2/GPT-2-class model — on a narrow task like instruction-style SFT on a small dataset. Write the LoRA layer yourself, inject it into attention projections (start with q and v, then try k, o, and MLP projections), keep the base weights frozen, and verify that only A and B receive gradients. Then add the practical pieces: saving/loading adapter weights only, merging LoRA into the base weights for inference, and comparing merged vs. unmerged outputs. Only after that works should you move to the rented GPU and a larger open model. The context is consistent with this being realistic: LoRA is widely used across the ecosystem (Fireworks AI, Together AI, Thinking Machines Lab, SGLang, and various SDXL/ControlNet LoRA projects are all listed as using it, though those are mostly “claimed” rather than independently verified), and one anecdotal report claims a 7B model was LoRA-trained in ~90 minutes for under a dollar on Runpod — treat that as a data point, not a guarantee. Fireworks’ own docs note you need a dataset, a supported base model, and GPU quota, and that they support major open families like Llama, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM; that’s useful if you want a managed comparison point, but for a capstone, doing it yourself is the point.

For experiments that demonstrate understanding, aim for ablations rather than a single fine-tune: (1) rank sweep r ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32, 64} and plot quality vs. trainable-parameter count and memory; (2) alpha/r scaling ablation; (3) target-module ablation (q/v only vs. all attention vs. attention+MLP); (4) LoRA vs. full fine-tuning vs. no training on the same data, measuring both task metrics and forgetting on a held-out general benchmark; (5) merged vs. unmerged inference equivalence and latency; (6) learning-rate sensitivity, since LoRA often tolerates higher LR than full FT; (7) adapter size on disk vs. base model size; (8) a failure-mode analysis — e.g., underfitting at tiny r, overfitting on small data, or degradation when the task requires knowledge the base model lacks. If you can explain why each curve looks the way it does, you understand LoRA.

A rough 10-week plan: weeks 1–2, PyTorch + transformer internals refresher and reproduce a tiny training loop; weeks 3–4, implement and unit-test your LoRA layer (gradient flow, freeze check, merge correctness); weeks 5–6, laptop-scale fine-tune and first ablations; weeks 7–8, rented-GPU run on a 1–7B open model with the full experiment matrix; weeks 9–10, analysis, write-up, and a clean repo with a from-scratch implementation plus a PEFT-based baseline for comparison. One caution: the ecosystem facts above (e.g., Thinking Machines Lab’s Inkling 2 Small being integrated with Unsloth/SGLang/vLLM and post-trainable with Miles/SkyRL) are mostly self-claimed or vendor-reported, so cite them as such if you mention them. Also note that “LoRA works well” is task-dependent — your capstone will be stronger if you include a case where LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning and explain why.

prose:
Great capstone choice — LoRA is small enough to implement from scratch but deep enough to show real understanding. Here's a plan grounded in what's in the graph.

**What to learn first (weeks 1–3).** LoRA is a subtype of PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning) and of fine-tuning generally, so build the foundations in that order: (1) transformer internals — attention, linear layers, backprop, mixed precision; (2) full fine-tuning vs. PEFT, and why post-training datasets are small relative to base-model scale; (3) the LoRA paper itself (Hu et al., 2021, "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models") — low-rank decomposition of weight updates, the A/B matrices, rank r, alpha scaling, and which modules to target (attention projections vs. MLP). Also read Thinking Machines Lab's "LoRA Without Regret" (thinkingmachines.ai/blog/lora/), which is the best recent empirical guide: it finds LoRA can match full fine-tuning's sample efficiency and final performance when key details are right, and that LoRA has sufficient capacity for typical post-training dataset sizes. Note their caveat that LoRA lags full FT on high-volume datasets — that's a great hypothesis to test. Also skim QLoRA (quantized LoRA) since it's what makes single-GPU work feasible.

**What to build (weeks 3–7).** Implement LoRA yourself rather than only calling a library: a minimal PyTorch implementation that injects low-rank adapters into nn.Linear layers of a small model (e.g., a GPT-2-scale or a small Llama/Qwen-class model), with correct initialization (A ~ Gaussian, B = 0 so the adapter starts as identity), alpha/r scaling, and merge/unmerge for inference. Then reproduce the same run with Hugging Face PEFT + a quantized base (QLoRA-style) as your "industry baseline" — the graph shows Hugging Face, Together AI, Fireworks AI, Modal, SGLang and Thinking Machines Lab all use LoRA in practice, so matching the standard tooling matters. Deliverable: a clean repo with your from-scratch implementation, the PEFT baseline, and a short writeup.

**Experiments that show understanding (weeks 6–10).**
- Rank sweep: r ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32, 64} — plot loss/eval vs. trainable params; find where returns diminish.
- LoRA vs. full fine-tuning vs. QLoRA on the same small dataset and budget — compare final loss, sample efficiency, wall-clock, and memory. This directly replicates the "LoRA Without Regret" question.
- Target-module ablation: attention-only vs. attention+MLP; measure effect.
- Data-size scaling: subsample your dataset (e.g., 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) and check whether LoRA matches full FT at small scale but lags at large scale, as the Thinking Machines results suggest.
- Log loss rather than only sampling-based evals — cleaner signal, as they note.
- Practical extras: adapter merge correctness check (merged model == base + adapter output), and a tiny multi-adapter serving demo if time permits.

**Practical notes.** On a laptop, do everything except final training runs there (data prep, unit tests, small-model debugging). Use the rented GPU for the sweeps; keep runs short with a small model and a modest instruction dataset. Budget roughly: 3 weeks learning + implementation, 4 weeks experiments, 2 weeks writeup, 1 week buffer. Pitfalls to avoid: forgetting B=0 init, applying LoRA to the wrong modules, comparing against full FT with mismatched hyperparameters, and reporting only one seed.

One honest caveat: the graph's evidence on LoRA is mostly "claimed" rather than verified, and the strongest empirical source is the Thinking Machines blog — treat its conclusions as hypotheses your capstone can probe, not settled fact. That framing ("I reproduced/tested these claims") is exactly what makes a capstone impressive.

Here's what the graph shows, plus my advice.

**Graph findings**
- LoRA (method:lora) is a subtype of PEFT and of fine-tuning (both claimed, single-source, e.g. Thinking Machines' blog calling LoRA "the leading PEFT method"). It's one of the most-used methods in the graph: 20 inbound uses_method edges, behind RL (38) and fine-tuning (22), ahead of SFT (17). Users include Thinking Machines Lab, Together AI, Surge AI, Fireworks AI, Modal, Hugging Face, SGLang, CoreWeave Forge, and many SDXL/FLUX image-model adapters.
- Hugging Face's own blog describes training LoRA adapters on Qwen models and testing LoRAs for 3D fine-tuning (self-claimed).

- "experiments" as a method has 0 edges — no graph support; experiments are your own design, not a named method.

**Advice (10 weeks, laptop + one rented GPU)**
- Learn first: linear algebra of low-rank matrices, backprop, transformer attention, then fine-tuning vs PEFT vs LoRA (rank r, alpha, target modules, merge/unmerge). Read the LoRA paper and a PEFT library (Hugging Face PEFT — HF is a confirmed LoRA user in the graph).
- Build: (1) a from-scratch LoRA layer in PyTorch (inject A/B into attention projections, freeze base, train only adapters); (2) the same via HF PEFT on a small open model; (3) merge adapters back and verify outputs match.
- Experiments that show understanding: rank sweep (r=4/8/16/64) vs quality and trainable-param count; target-module ablation (q/v only vs all linear); LoRA vs full fine-tune vs frozen baseline on a small benchmark; adapter merge correctness check; overfitting/data-size curve; optionally QLoRA-style 4-bit if GPU memory is tight (note: not covered in graph).
- Ground it in practice: replicate what HF/Together AI-style shops do — small adapter on a Qwen-class model, evaluate on a held-out set, report params trained and wall-clock.

Caveats: all LoRA edges are "claimed" status, mostly self-reported; the graph is a sample, so absence (QLoRA, experiments) isn't proof of irrelevance.

question: We're a 20-person startup with an LLM agent in production. Should we post-train our own model with RL instead of prompting a frontier API? Which companies do this as a service or in-house today, which methods do they use, and what would a two-week go/no-go prototype look like?

Which specific methods and variants do those organisations use (e.g., RLHF, DPO, PPO, GRPO, RLAIF), and which tools/platforms do they rely on for RL post-training?
Which models in the graph were built or improved via RL post-training, and which benchmarks are used to measure the gains (e.g., agentic/tool-use or reasoning benchmarks)?
Which datasets and evaluation setups are used for RL post-training of agents, and which organisations publish or offer them?
Which roles do organisations hire for RL post-training / LLM alignment work, and at what scale — i.e., is this feasible for a 20-person startup or only for labs with dedicated teams?
Which organisations offer RL post-training or fine-tuning as a service (managed platforms, API-based fine-tuning, alignment vendors) that a startup could buy instead of building in-house?

notes.finding: Applied Compute is a dedicated RL post-training vendor for open models on customer data, backed by Sequoia/Benchmark/NVIDIA and partnered with Cognition; it uses GRPO, online RL, full-parameter RL, LLM-as-a-judge and self-distillation, and offers an Agent Cloud plus AC2 infrastructure.
notes.implication: Shortlist Applied Compute as a buy-side partner for a two-week pilot; ask for a reference customer and a scoped eval before committing.

notes.finding: Together AI offers 'Together Post-Training' (self-claimed) and uses GRPO, DPO and PPO; it also ships agentic models (HybridAgent-8B/14B-Agentic) and agentic datasets (CoderForge-Preview, HybridAgent-HybridSFT-v2, SWE-bench Verified trajectories).
notes.implication: Use Together as the fastest path to a GRPO/DPO experiment on an open base model; reuse its CoderForge/SWE-bench-style data as a template for your own agentic eval set.

notes.finding: Fireworks AI offers a 'Fireworks Training API' to run your own RL loop (self-claimed), works on 'reinforcement learning at scale', and uses GRPO and DPO; it hires Member of Technical Staff roles in AI Training Infrastructure and Applied ML.
notes.implication: If you want to keep the training loop in-house but rent the infra, prototype on the Fireworks Training API rather than building RL infrastructure from scratch.

notes.finding: CoreWeave Forge (offered by CoreWeave and Mistral) is a managed post-training platform using RLHF, DPO, LoRA and distillation, with confirmed enterprise users Pinterest, MasterClass and Walden Robotics — one of the few service claims with customer-side confirmation.
notes.implication: Treat CoreWeave Forge as the lower-risk managed option; its confirmed customer edges make it a better reference-check candidate than purely self-claimed vendors.

notes.finding: Mercor post-trains open models with small expert-labeled datasets (fewer than 1,000 tasks nearly doubled an open model's APEX-Agents score; ~2,000 scaled further), using RL with SkyRL and LLM-judge/human-expert review; its AC-Small (GLM-4.7) rose from 17th to 4th on APEX-Agents.
notes.implication: Build a 100–500 task expert-labeled eval/training set for your own agent workflow — the graph suggests data quality, not scale, is the lever; this is a concrete two-week project.

notes.finding: Surge AI offers RLHF as a service (self-claimed) and publishes post-training research on agentic tasks (Kimi-K2.7 on GDP.pdf, cross-benchmark RL transfer on agentic coding); it serves Microsoft and partners with Meta Superintelligence Labs, and offers benchmarks like GDP.pdf, DAYJOB and HANDBOOK.md.
notes.implication: If your bottleneck is expert data and reward design rather than compute, Surge-style data+RLHF services are the buy option; use their published GDP.pdf/DAYJOB methodology as a template for long-horizon agent evals.

notes.finding: In-house RL post-training is concentrated in labs and well-funded teams: Anthropic (RLHF), Thinking Machines Lab, Hugging Face and vLLM (GRPO), Zyphra (ZONOS3-Mini via DPO+GRPO), Cognition (SWE-1.7, RL on a Kimi K2.7 base); Applied Compute hires Research Scientists and Research/Platform Engineers, i.e., dedicated teams.
notes.implication: A 20-person startup should not staff an in-house RL team; the skill to build is eval design and vendor management, not RL infrastructure — exploit the gap by being a sophisticated buyer.

notes.finding: Agentic RL gains are measured on tool-use/reasoning benchmarks — APEX-Agents, Toolathlon (600+ tools), GDPval, SWE-bench Verified — and Together/Fireworks/Surge publish relevant datasets (CoderForge, bfcl_v3_multi_turn_base, GDP.pdf), but nearly all vendor service claims in the graph are self-claimed (strength 0.5) with few customer-side confirmations.
notes.implication: Before any go/no-go, build your own held-out agentic eval (tool-use + verifiable checks) and demand benchmark evidence plus reference customers from vendors — don't trust self-claimed leaderboard numbers.

prose:
Here's what the graph shows, organized by your sub-questions.

**1. Who does RL post-training (in-house or as a service)**
- **Applied Compute** — RL post-training of open models on customer data; heavy investor backing (Sequoia, Benchmark, NVIDIA, Kleiner Perkins), partners with Cognition; offers "Applied Compute Agent Cloud", AC2, Context Engine; works on multi-turn agentic workloads.
- **Mercor** — post-trains open models (e.g., Qwen3.5-397B, GLM-4.7 → "AC-Small") with expert data; publishes APEX-Agents benchmark work; uses SkyRL-style RL training.
- **Surge AI** — offers RLHF as a service plus post-training research (Kimi-K2.7 on GDP.pdf, cross-benchmark RL transfer on agentic coding); serves Microsoft; partners with Meta Superintelligence Labs.
- **Together AI** — "Together Post-Training" service (self-claimed); uses GRPO/DPO/PPO; offers HybridAgent agentic models and CoderForge datasets.
- **Fireworks AI** — "Fireworks Training API" for running your own RL loop (self-claimed); works on "reinforcement learning at scale"; uses GRPO/DPO.
- **CoreWeave Forge** (CoreWeave, also offered by Mistral) — managed post-training: RLHF, DPO, LoRA, distillation; used by Pinterest, MasterClass, Walden Robotics.
- **In-house labs**: Anthropic (RLHF), Thinking Machines Lab (GRPO), Hugging Face (GRPO), vLLM (GRPO), Zyphra (ZONOS3-Mini via DPO+GRPO), Cognition (SWE-1.7, RL pipeline on Kimi K2.7 base).

**2. Methods and tools**
GRPO is the most-cited variant (Together, Applied Compute, Surge, Fireworks, Thinking Machines, HF, vLLM, Zyphra); DPO (Together, Fireworks, CoreWeave Forge, Zyphra); PPO (Together); RLHF (Anthropic, Surge, CoreWeave Forge); plus online RL, full-parameter RL, LLM-as-a-judge, self-distillation (Applied Compute). Tools/platforms: Fireworks Training API, Together Post-Training, CoreWeave Forge, SkyRL (Mercor), vLLM. Note: nearly all service claims are self-claims (strength 0.5); customer-side confirmations exist for CoreWeave Forge (Pinterest, MasterClass) and partnerships (Cognition–Applied Compute).

**3. Models and benchmarks**
ZONOS3-Mini (DPO+GRPO); Mercor's AC-Small (GLM-4.7 post-trained, 17th→4th on APEX-Agents); Cognition SWE-1.7 (RL on Kimi K2.7 base); Together HybridAgent-8B/14B-Agentic. Benchmarks: APEX-Agents, Toolathlon (600+ tools), GDPval, SWE-bench Verified (CoderForge trajectories), Surge's GDP.pdf/DAYJOB/HANDBOOK.md/sudo L7.

**4. Datasets/eval setups**
Together: CoderForge-Preview, HybridAgent-HybridSFT-v2, SWE-bench Verified trajectories. Surge: GDP.pdf, DAYJOB, Chartography, Handbook-v1.1. Mercor: APEX-Agents dev set (~1–2k expert-labeled tasks nearly doubled open-model scores). Fireworks: bfcl_v3_multi_turn_base (function calling). Applied Compute: Contextbase.

**5. Roles and scale**
Applied Compute hires Research Scientists, Applied/Platform Research Engineers, Research Systems Engineers, AI Platform Engineers, Compute Analysts. Fireworks hires Member of Technical Staff (AI Training Infrastructure, Applied ML). Mercor hires Research Scientist (APEX Benchmarks), Software Engineer (Agent Platform). This is dedicated-team territory — but the *service* route exists precisely so a 20-person startup doesn't need it.

**6. Buy-vs-build**
Buy: Together Post-Training, Fireworks Training API, CoreWeave Forge, Surge AI (data + RLHF), Applied Compute (full-service RL post-training), Mercor (expert data + post-training).

**Bottom line for a 20-person startup:** don't build in-house RL infra. Run a two-week go/no-go: (1) days 1–3, pick one high-volume agentic workflow, build a small eval (50–200 tasks, LLM-judge + verifiable checks, à la APEX/SWE-bench style); (2) days 4–7, baseline the frontier API and one open model (e.g., a Qwen/GLM-class base) with prompting only; (3) days 8–12, run one cheap post-training pass via a vendor (Fireworks Training API or Together Post-Training with GRPO/DPO, or Surge/Mercor-style expert data if quality is the bottleneck); (4) days 13–14, compare on held-out tasks + cost/latency. Go only if the tuned open model beats the API baseline on your eval by a margin that pays back inference savings; otherwise stay on the API. Caveats: graph evidence for vendor claims is mostly self-reported; validate with a paid pilot and reference customers.

question: We're a 20-person startup with an LLM agent in production. Should we post-train our own model with RL instead of prompting a frontier API? Which companies do this as a service or in-house today, which methods do they use, and what would a two-week go/no-go prototype look like?

notes.finding: RadixArk trains models with reinforcement learning (via 'Miles'), corroborated by two independent publishers (radixark.com and huggingface.co). This is one of the few non-self-claimed RL post-training signals in the graph.
notes.implication: Study RadixArk's published post-training write-ups as a concrete reference architecture before committing to in-house RL.

notes.finding: Abundant builds reinforcement learning environments and datasets (running on Modal Sandboxes), corroborated across modal.com and abundant.ai. They sell the environment/data layer rather than finished models.
notes.implication: For a 20-person team, buying RL environments/data from a vendor like Abundant is more realistic than building them; evaluate them as a prototype partner.

notes.finding: Cognition (SWE-1.5/1.6), Surge AI (RL-only post-training of Kimi K2.7 Code on 1,700 expert agentic coding tasks; Nemotron 3.5 Super VL), and Applied Compute (DoorDash, Cognition, Mercor case studies) all claim RL post-training work, but evidence is self-claimed or unverified aggregator quotes.
notes.implication: Treat vendor case studies as leads, not proof; in a go/no-go, demand a paid pilot with your own evals rather than trusting published benchmarks.

notes.finding: Baseten claims support for SFT and RL workloads, and CoreWeave Forge claims RLHF plus distillation (via Mistral's Forge page). These are platform/service routes to RL post-training without owning GPU infrastructure.
notes.implication: Use a managed platform (Baseten or CoreWeave Forge) for the two-week prototype instead of standing up training infra.

notes.finding: GRPO is the dominant named RL method in the graph: claimed by Together AI, Applied Compute, Surge AI, Hugging Face, Fireworks AI, Thinking Machines Lab, and vLLM. RLHF appears only for Anthropic and CoreWeave Forge (both claimed); RLAIF has no edges in the graph.
notes.implication: Learn GRPO (and its tooling in vLLM/Hugging Face) as the default method for the prototype; skip RLAIF since the graph shows no adoption signal.

notes.finding: Anthropic's RLHF use is claimed but weakly sourced (one self-source unverified, one aggregator); no corroborated frontier-lab RLHF edge exists in the graph. Most RL edges overall are 'claimed' status with self-reported sources.
notes.implication: Don't anchor your decision on frontier-lab precedent; the graph can't confirm how they do it, so validate methods on your own task.

notes.finding: The graph shows RL post-training concentrated in (a) frontier/product labs doing it in-house (Cognition, Reka, Reflection, Microsoft, RadixArk) and (b) specialist vendors selling it as a service (Surge AI, Applied Compute, Abundant, Baseten, CoreWeave Forge). No graph evidence shows small startups succeeding with fully in-house RL.
notes.implication: Default plan: keep the frontier API as baseline and rent RL capability (vendor or managed platform) for the prototype; only consider in-house if the pilot shows clear ROI.

notes.finding: A viable two-week go/no-go (synthesis, not a graph fact): pick one narrow agent task with a programmatic/verifiable reward, assemble ~100-500 graded examples, run GRPO on a small open model via Baseten/Fireworks/Together or with Abundant/Surge/Applied Compute environments, and compare task success, cost, and latency against the prompted frontier API on held-out cases.
notes.implication: Build the eval harness and reward function first (week 1); if you can't define a verifiable reward or the RL model doesn't beat the API baseline, the answer is no-go and you stay on prompting.

changes.what: Added managed platforms and specialist vendors (Baseten, CoreWeave Forge, Abundant, Surge AI, Applied Compute) as the preferred route for the two-week spike instead of in-house RL infrastructure.
Added Abundant as a source of RL environments/datasets (corroborated, runs on Modal Sandboxes) for the prototype.

Flagged Anthropic's RLHF use as weakly sourced (self-source unverified); do not anchor the plan on frontier-lab precedent.
Reordered online RL learning to GRPO-first (most-named method across Together AI, Fireworks AI, Hugging Face, Thinking Machines Lab, vLLM, Applied Compute, Surge AI) ahead of PPO.
No adoption signal for RLAIF anywhere in the ecosystem; dropped it implicitly by keeping preference optimization to DPO/IPO/KTO and online RL to GRPO/PPO.
Added RadixArk (corroborated RL via 'Miles') as a reference implementation to study before committing.

No evidence of small startups succeeding with fully in-house RL; the observed pattern is frontier labs in-house vs vendors-as-a-service, so the plan defaults to renting capability and only going in-house after a positive pilot.
Made the two-week go/no-go explicitly a three-way comparison (frontier API vs SFT vs GRPO/RLVR spike) with a verifier-first gate, matching the synthesis finding.

draft.summary: For a 20-person startup, RL post-training is usually a later-stage lever, not the first fix: exhaust prompting, tool/scaffold design, RAG, and SFT before online RL. RL is worth a prototype only when you have a cheap, reliable verifier, high task volume, and measured plateau from simpler methods. A two-week go/no-go should compare frontier API, SFT open model, and a small GRPO/RLVR spike on one narrow task slice.

prose:
Here's what the graph supports, with gaps flagged.

**1. Open base models with derivatives.** The graph is thin on explicit `builds_on` edges for LLMs — most derivative edges cluster around image models (SDXL LoRAs, FLUX). The one verified LLM derivative edge I found is Qwen-SEA-LION-v4.5-27B-IT-GGUF → Qwen (derivation: quantize). Llama 3 / Llama 2 / Mistral show no inbound `builds_on` edges in the graph, though they're the most-referenced open bases in text (Replicate, Fireworks, Quora all reference Llama/Mistral). So: Llama and Qwen are the de facto open bases people build on; the graph just doesn't count derivatives well.

**2. What derivatives change.** Methods: fine-tuning (used by Arcee AI, Thinking Machines Lab, Together AI, Scale AI, Cisco, Lyft, etc.), LoRA (Thinking Machines, Together AI, Fireworks, Hugging Face, CoreWeave Forge, Baseten-adjacent tooling), SFT (Together AI, Baseten, Fireworks, Modal, CoreWeave Model Distillation — confirmed), QLoRA (no edges). Derivatives typically change adapters/quantization rather than full weights. Training datasets: I didn't get to enumerate `trained_on` edges — not covered.

**3. Fine-tuning tooling/platforms.** Thinking Machines Lab offers Tinker (claimed); Baseten offers Baseten Loops (claimed, used by LangChain to train custom models for LangSmith Engine); CoreWeave Forge and CoreWeave Model Distillation (LoRA/SFT, one confirmed); Together AI post-training/fine-tuning; Fireworks AI; Replicate; Modal; Arcee AI. Technologies use LoRA and SFT most.

**4. Benchmarks.** Not explored — no `measured_on` edges pulled. Not in the graph from my queries; you'd want to check MMLU/HumanEval-style edges directly.

**5. Hiring.** `hires_for` queries for ML engineer roles returned nothing usable — not in the graph from my queries. Signal from elsewhere: many orgs (Together, Fireworks, Baseten) sell fine-tuning as a service with forward-deployed engineers, i.e., vendor-managed is common; in-house ownership means hiring ML/MLOps engineers, which the graph doesn't quantify.

**6. Enterprise assistants / domain adaptation.** Glean, Cohere, Infor work on Enterprise AI; LangChain works on AI agents. Cohere is the clearest "enterprise assistant + domain adaptation" player. Partners/services: Together AI serves Notion, Sourcegraph, Genspark, Arcee AI; Baseten serves LangChain; Fireworks serves Notion/Sourcegraph.

**Bottom line for your project:** pick Llama 3 or Qwen as the open base, fine-tune with LoRA/SFT (the dominant, cheapest pattern), own it via an internal pipeline (Tinker, CoreWeave Forge, or Together/Baseten if you want vendor help), and prove it with a held-out internal eval plus a standard benchmark — though benchmark edges weren't verifiable in the graph. Caveat: several edges are "claimed" not "verified/confirmed," and derivative-count and hiring data are weak in this graph.
Evidence check done — here's what the sources actually say, and how much weight each edge deserves:

- **Qwen-SEA-LION-v4.5-27B-IT-GGUF builds_on Qwen** — *verified*, independent primary record (Hugging Face model card, `base_model:quantized:aisingapore/Qwen-SEA-LION-v4.5-27B-IT`), entailment-checked. This is the strongest edge I have: it confirms Qwen derivatives exist and that quantization is a typical derivative change. It does **not** prove Qwen is the most-derived base overall — the graph just lacks counted `builds_on` edges for Llama/Mistral.
- **Thinking Machines Lab offers Tinker** — *claimed*, self-published only ("we are launching Tinker, a flexible API for fine-tuning language models"), and two citations were dropped for not supporting the claim. Treat as a real product announcement, not independently verified.
- **CoreWeave Model Distillation uses SFT** — *confirmed* by the counterparty ("It uses supervised fine-tuning to train a smaller open-weight model"). Solid support for "SFT is a standard fine-tuning method in production tooling."
- **Baseten offers Baseten Loops** — *claimed*, self-claim only ("managed infrastructure for fine-tuning models through an API"). Real offering per Baseten's own site, but unverified externally; the LangChain customer story is also Baseten-published.
- **Glean works_on Enterprise AI** — *claimed*, self-claim ("The enterprise AI platform that puts company context to work"). Directionally useful, not independent proof.

Net effect on my advice: the recommendation to fine-tune an open base (Llama 3 / Qwen) with LoRA/SFT stands, but the tooling names (Tinker, Baseten Loops, CoreWeave Forge/Distillation) are vendor self-claims — evaluate them hands-on rather than trusting the graph. The one hard fact is the verified Qwen derivative edge; benchmark and hiring questions remain unanswered in the graph, so "prove it worked" needs your own held-out eval plus a standard benchmark you run yourself.

notes.finding: Cognition (Devin/SWE-1.6/Kevin-32B) is the clearest agentic-RL practitioner in the graph: it self-claims agentic RL, async RL and mid-training; Kevin-32B is a verified fine-tune of QwQ-32B trained with RL, and SWE-1.6 is measured on SWE-bench Pro vs SWE-1.5.
notes.implication: Study Cognition's public write-ups (SWE-1.6 preview, Kevin-32B) as your reference architecture for agentic RL on coding; replicate a small async-RL loop on a Qwen/QwQ-class base as a team project.

notes.finding: GRPO is the most-cited RL variant across the graph (Together AI, Applied Compute, Surge AI, Fireworks AI, Thinking Machines, Hugging Face, vLLM), alongside RLVR (Surge AI post-trained Qwen3-4B Thinking), rubric-rewarded RL, and full-parameter/online RL (Applied Compute).
notes.implication: Make GRPO + RLVR with verifiable (execution-based) rewards your default recipe; learn it hands-on rather than PPO, and treat rubric/LLM-judge rewards as a secondary experiment arm.

notes.finding: Poolside trains with Reinforcement Learning from Code Execution Feedback (RLCEF) — execution-grounded rewards for coding — and is served/partnered by Baseten; the claim is self-reported via an aggregator source.
entities: Reinforcement Learning from Code Execution Feedback
notes.implication: Build an execution-feedback reward harness (run tests in a sandbox, reward pass/fail) — this is the highest-signal, most reproducible reward design for coding agents and a concrete project for the quarter.

notes.finding: Infrastructure for agentic RL is productized: CoreWeave Forge offers RL/RLHF/distillation/LoRA training (used by Pinterest, MasterClass, Walden Robotics; co-offered with Mistral), Deeptune (acquired by Mercor) sells high-fidelity RL training gyms/simulations, and Cognition runs on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 + Cerebras Inference + NVIDIA Dynamo.
notes.implication: Don't build orchestration from scratch: evaluate CoreWeave Forge or Modal + vLLM for rollouts, and use sandboxed execution environments (Deeptune-style gyms) as your RL environment layer.

notes.finding: SWE-bench Pro is the de facto coding-agent RL benchmark in the graph (SWE-1.6, Kimi K2.7 Code, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, Surge AI all measured on it), with Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Marathon as secondary evals and FrontierCode positioned against SWE-bench Pro.
notes.implication: Standardize your eval harness on SWE-bench Pro + Terminal-Bench 2.1 so results are comparable to published numbers; treat FrontierCode as a contamination-resistant cross-check.

notes.finding: Reported comparisons are mostly new-model-vs-prior-version (SWE-1.6 vs SWE-1.5) and vs frontier closed models (Kimi K2.7 Code vs Claude Fable 5); explicit SFT-only vs RL ablations and reward-design ablations are essentially absent from the graph — a clear gap.
notes.implication: Exploit the gap: run controlled ablations (SFT-only vs SFT+GRPO, execution reward vs rubric/LLM-judge reward, base-model size sweep) — publishable, decision-useful results your team can't get from the literature.

CoreWeave Forge, Miles and Tailored Generation use it inside their platforms.

**2. Methods/variants.** LoRA and Multi-LoRA exist as distinct entities; QLoRA exists but has no edges in the graph (not covered). Prefix tuning isn't in the graph either. Thinking Machines' "LoRA Without Regret" is the key reading: with the right details, LoRA matches full fine-tuning's sample efficiency and final performance at typical post-training dataset sizes.

**3. Tools/platforms.** Hugging Face (PEFT ecosystem, self-claim), Together AI post-training (LoRA incl. multi-adapter on shared GPU), Modal (training infra, SFT/RL), CoreWeave Forge, Miles, Tailored Generation, SGLang and vLLM-style inference engines support multi-LoRA serving (per the Thinking Machines article).

**4. Models/datasets/benchmarks.** LoRA-built models in the graph are mostly image-side: SDXL ControlNet LoRA variants, sdxl-outpainting-lora, sdxl-lcm-lora-controlnet, FLUX 3 Image Klein, Photorealistic FX. On the LLM side, Hugging Face trained LoRA adapters on Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B. No LoRA-specific dataset edges found; evaluation benchmarks are generic (below).

**5. Roles.** Direct "hires_for LoRA" edges don't exist; closest is Databricks offering Machine Learning Engineer roles, and Together AI's forward-deployed engineers doing post-training (data, training environments, evals, shipping endpoints). prose:
Here's what I verified in the graph, then my advice.

**Graph check results**
- **LoRA** (`method:lora`) exists; it's a subtype of **PEFT** (`method:peft`) — edge `method:lora|subtype_of|method:peft`, status *claimed*, strength 0.5, sourced to a Thinking Machines blog ("The leading PEFT method is low-rank adaptation, or LoRA."). Treat as claimed, not verified.
- LoRA is widely used in practice: Hugging Face uses it (edge `org:hugging-face|uses_method|method:lora`, *claimed*, self-sourced — e.g., LoRA adapters on Qwen models), as do Thinking Machines Lab, Together AI, Fireworks AI, Modal, SGLang, CoreWeave Forge, and others (all *claimed*, strength 0.5).
- **QLoRA** (`method:qlora`) exists as an entity but has **no edges** in the graph — nothing to confirm about it there.
- **MMLU** (`benchmark:mmlu`) exists as a benchmark entity (also MMLU-Pro, Global MMLU); I didn't find LoRA-specific benchmark edges to rely on.
- No graph entries for a canonical "LoRA paper" or specific learning curricula — so the study plan below is my advice, not graph-sourced.

**Advice (10 weeks, laptop + one rented GPU)**

*Learn first (weeks 1–2):* linear algebra of low-rank matrices (SVD, rank, why ΔW = BA with r ≪ d works), transformer attention/MLP block structure, backprop, and PyTorch autograd. Then read the LoRA paper and the PEFT framing (graph confirms LoRA sits under PEFT). Skim QLoRA conceptually (4-bit base + LoRA) even though the graph has no edges on it.

*Build (weeks 3–6):* implement LoRA from scratch — a `LoRALinear` layer wrapping a frozen linear layer with A/B matrices, correct init (A random, B zero so ΔW=0 at start), scaling α/r, and merge/unmerge for inference. Apply it to attention projections (q, v) of a small model (e.g., a small GPT-2-class or Qwen-class model). Then compare against Hugging Face PEFT's implementation as a reference — the graph shows HF actively uses LoRA, so it's a sensible baseline.

*Experiments that show understanding (weeks 7–10):*
1. Rank sweep (r = 1, 4, 8, 16, 64): plot trainable params vs. task performance — show the low-rank hypothesis empirically.
2. Which modules to adapt (q/v only vs. all linear layers).
3. LoRA vs. full fine-tuning vs. frozen baseline on a small task; report MMLU or a task-specific eval (MMLU exists in the graph as a standard benchmark).
4. Ablations: α/r scaling, init scheme, merge vs. no-merge inference equivalence.
5. Memory/throughput comparison — this is where QLoRA-style quantization fits if your GPU is small.

*Capstone framing:* the strongest signal of understanding is the from-scratch implementation plus controlled ablations, not just "I fine-tuned a model." Keep everything reproducible (seeds, configs).

Caveat: graph evidence for LoRA's adoption is mostly *claimed*/*self-reported*, and QLoRA is unconnected in the graph — so verify paper details from primary sources yourself.

prose:
I have enough to answer. Summary of findings:

**Who does RL post-training (in-house / as a service):**
- In-house: Anthropic (RLHF, claimed, self + aggregator sources), Thinking Machines Lab, Hugging Face, vLLM, Applied Compute (all GRPO, claimed/self). Reflection hires for "Member of Technical Staff – Post-Training" (claimed).
- As a service/platform: Together AI (GRPO/PPO/DPO post-training, self-claimed), Fireworks AI (DPO/GRPO), CoreWeave Forge (RLHF/DPO), Surge AI (offers RLHF, uses GRPO — data/labeling side), NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (GRPO, infra). All edges are "claimed" (single-source, mostly self-published); nothing corroborated/verified in the graph.

**Methods/tools:** GRPO is the most-linked method (Together, Applied Compute, Surge, vLLM, HF, Fireworks, Thinking Machines, NVIDIA); DPO (Together, Fireworks, CoreWeave Forge, ZONOS3-Mini); RLHF (Anthropic, Surge, CoreWeave Forge); RLAIF has no edges. ZONOS3-Mini is a model post-trained with DPO+GRPO.

**Evidence RL beats prompting a frontier API for agents:** Not in the graph — no benchmark edges comparing RL-post-trained vs prompted frontier models on agent tasks were found; Together's GRPO claim is on GSM8K (math, not agents). Treat "RL > prompting" as unproven here.

**Datasets/benchmarks for preference/RL:** Not surfaced as startup-accessible offers in the graph; no strong offers/publishes edges found for preference datasets.

**Frontier alternative:** org:frontier-ai is served by Mercor (claimed); frontier labs (Anthropic etc.) offer the API you'd be replacing — you'd give up their capability, safety tooling, and zero-ops scaling.

**Recommendation / two-week go/no-go prototype:** Don't self-train from scratch. Week 1: pick a narrow, high-volume agent task with a verifiable reward; baseline a frontier API with your best prompt; collect ~500–2k preference/trajectory examples; try Together AI or Fireworks post-training (GRPO/DPO) on an open base model. Week 2: eval on held-out agent tasks vs the prompted frontier baseline (success rate, cost/task, latency). Go only if ≥20–30% cost reduction or clear quality win at acceptable latency; otherwise stay on the API. Note all vendor claims are self-reported — demand a paid pilot with your data before committing.

RL only pays off with a reliable reward signal and enough task volume — otherwise prompting/SFT wins.

notes.finding: Qwen3.8-27B is the most-derived open base in the graph (26 derivatives, e.g. DaisyRose-27B, corroborated by 2 publishers); Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, Qwen3.5-9B/4B and Qwen3-8B follow, with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7) and gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (6) as non-Qwen options.
notes.implication: Pick Qwen3-8B (small, cheap) or Qwen3.8-27B (max headroom) as the base; learn the Qwen fine-tuning stack and its derivative ecosystem rather than starting from a Llama-only mental model.

notes.finding: Derivatives mostly adapt rather than retrain: quantizations (NVFP4/FP8/GGUF/AWQ), SFT/instruct variants and speculative-decoding heads dominate the builds_on edges.
notes.implication: Plan the project as LoRA/SFT + quantization for serving, not full pretraining; learn GGUF/AWQ/NVFP4 packaging as a deliverable skill.

prose:
Here's what the graph shows, with caveats (it's a ~1,900-page sample, not the whole field):

**1. Open base models people build on.** The most-derived bases are Qwen-family: Qwen3.8-27B (26 derivatives, e.g. DaisyRose-27B — corroborated by RadixArk + Hugging Face), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (8), Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (8, vision/OCR), Qwen3.5-9B/4B (6 each), Qwen3-8B (6). Also Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7), gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (6), GPT-OSS-120B (5). Derivatives are mostly quantizations (NVFP4/FP8/GGUF/AWQ), SFT/instruct variants, and speculative-decoding heads — i.e., people mostly adapt rather than retrain.

**2. What derivatives change.** Methods: fine-tuning (22 users incl. Arcee AI, Thinking Machines Lab, Replicate), LoRA (20; Thinking Machines, Together AI, Surge AI — Together's LoRA claim is self-claimed), SFT (17; Together AI, Baseten, CoreWeave Forge), GRPO (9), distillation (10), post-training (9), RL (38 overall). Datasets: mostly task/domain-specific (e.g. unbias-plus-dataset for Qwen SFT variants, hh-rlhf for preference tuning); general pretraining corpora (pile, RedPajama) appear for base models, not fine-tunes.

**3. Fine-tuning tooling/platforms.** Together AI offers Fine-Tuning (plus GPU clusters, dedicated endpoints) and uses LoRA/SFT/GRPO; CoreWeave Forge (SFT, distillation), Baseten, Fireworks AI, Replicate, Arcee AI, Thinking Machines Lab all appear as fine-tuning users/providers. Arcee AI and Thinking Machines are the most fine-tuning-centric orgs in the graph.

**4. Benchmarks to prove it worked.** No assistant-specific fine-tune benchmark dominates; the most-measured are DeepResearch Bench II (27), Terminal Bench 2.1 (8, incl. DaisyRose-27B), DeepSWE (8), SimpleQA (7), Multimodal RewardBench 2 (7). For an internal assistant, pair a general capability check (SimpleQA-style) with a task-specific eval you build; the graph has no "internal assistant" benchmark.

**5. Orgs/roles.** Anthropic works on assistant alignment; assistant-adjacent hiring skews to Forward Deployed Engineer (Surge AI, Reflection, OpenRouter), Software Engineer (Agent Platform) (Sierra, Browserbase, Mercor), Research Scientists (NVIDIA, Applied Compute, Anthropic). No org in the graph works on a literal "internal assistant" problem — that's a gap, not evidence it doesn't exist.

**6. Picking a base.** Qwen3.8-27B / Qwen3-8B / Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct have the deepest derivative ecosystems and evidence (corroborated builds_on edges, HF metadata). Llama-3.1-8B is the safest small pick; Qwen3.8-27B if you have the compute.

**Suggested project:** pick Qwen3-8B or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, LoRA/SFT on your internal Q&A + docs (RAG-augmented), serve via Together AI/Fireworks/Baseten or self-host, and prove it with a held-out internal eval plus SimpleQA/Terminal-Bench-style public checks, comparing base vs. fine-tune. Own it as the team's "internal assistant fine-tune" with a versioned eval harness. Caveat: most tooling edges are self-claims (claimed status); benchmark edges are stronger.

question: I'm a senior research engineer looking at RL for coding agents. Who is doing agentic RL in practice, which methods and infrastructure do they report, and which baselines and controlled experiments would be most informative for our team this quarter?
plan: Which organisations in the graph are linked to agentic RL (method:agentic-rl) or coding agents (technology:coding-agents), and what do they publish, offer or hire for?
Which methods and variants do those organisations report using (e.g. agentic RL vs. other RL/post-training methods), and with what status of evidence?
Which tools, platforms or infrastructure do they offer or use for coding agents and RL training (technologies, models, datasets)?
Which models were built or trained with agentic RL, and which benchmarks are they measured on (e.g. coding-agent evaluations)?
Which organisations hire for research engineers with RL/coding-agent focus, and what roles/skills do they list?
Which controlled experiments, baselines and comparisons are reported (model compares_against, org compares_against, benchmark results) that could anchor our team's evaluation plan?

notes.finding: Cognition is the only org in the graph explicitly linked to agentic RL, and it is self-claimed (single self-source: 'Since our early attempts at agentic RL, including Kevin-32B and SWE-grep'). Treat it as a lead, not settled fact.
notes.implication: Skill to learn: read Cognition's SWE-1.6/Kevin-32B posts closely and replicate their RL-for-coding setup; don't assume the field has converged on a recipe.

notes.finding: Kevin-32B is a verified fine-tune of QwQ-32B using RL (claimed), offered by Cognition (verified). This is the clearest concrete agentic-RL artifact in the graph: open base model + RL post-training for coding.
notes.implication: Project to build: reproduce a QwQ-32B-class RL fine-tune on a small coding-task set and measure the delta vs. the base model — a cheap, high-signal experiment.

notes.finding: SWE-1.6 is measured on SWE-bench Pro (corroborated, 2 publishers) at 50.4% vs SWE-1.5's 40.1% (~11% relative gain), and it compares directly against SWE-1.5. This is the best-supported benchmark comparison available for anchoring an eval plan.
notes.implication: Tool/benchmark to use: adopt SWE-bench Pro as your primary coding-agent eval and always report against a fixed prior checkpoint (SWE-1.5-style), not just absolute scores.

notes.finding: Cognition's stack pairs Cerebras Inference (confirmed) and NVIDIA Dynamo (corroborated) with a Cerebras partnership (corroborated) and an Applied Compute partnership (confirmed); SWE-1.6 itself uses Cerebras Inference (confirmed) and was reportedly trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 (claimed).
notes.implication: Gap to exploit: inference/training infra for RL rollouts is a differentiator — learn sandboxed rollout infra (Modal-style) and fast inference serving rather than only model code.

notes.finding: Modal is the infrastructure layer for coding-agent/RL workloads in the graph: it serves Markov Robotics and Ramp (both claimed), and its own materials describe sandboxes for coding agents and RL rollouts plus RL training on spin-up GPUs. Markov Robotics uses Modal Functions/Volumes/Tunnels and A100/H100s (all claimed).
notes.implication: Tool to use: prototype your RL rollout environment on Modal (or similar sandboxed GPU infra) — it's the pattern both a robotics lab and a fintech coding-agent team reportedly use.

notes.finding: Ramp works on coding agents (claimed) and built a background coding agent on Modal (per Modal's case study); it also uses Linear (confirmed). This shows coding agents are being adopted outside frontier labs, but evidence is self-reported/case-study grade.
notes.implication: Gap to exploit: applied coding-agent deployments (background agents in real workflows) are under-documented — a strong portfolio project is an internal background coding agent with measured task throughput.

notes.finding: Hiring signal in the graph is thin: only Anthropic → Research Engineers exists (claimed), with no RL/coding-agent-specific role or skills edges. Absence here means the graph doesn't cover it, not that demand is low.
notes.implication: Skill to learn: position yourself as a research engineer with RL + coding-agent eval experience (SWE-bench Pro, RL post-training, rollout infra) — the graph can't confirm specific job specs, so verify on live career pages.

notes.finding: Cognition's product surface (Devin, Windsurf, SWE-1.6, Kevin-32B) is corroborated or verified, and it has heavy investor backing (a16z, Founders Fund, Lux, Accel, etc., all confirmed) — but its agentic-RL method claims remain self-claimed, and Devin's comparison vs human engineers is weak (claimed, strength 0.3).
notes.implication: Implication: trust Cognition's shipped artifacts and benchmark deltas more than its method narrative; when evaluating vendors/baselines, demand independent reproductions rather than self-reported RL gains.

answer.summary: Focus this quarter on reproducible RL-for-coding-agent evaluation, not on chasing self-claimed method narratives. The best-supported anchors are Cognition's shipped artifacts and SWE-bench Pro comparison; the weakest evidence is around agentic-RL method claims and hiring/skills data. Build one controlled RL post-training reproduction and one background-agent prototype, and measure both against fixed baselines.
learn: RL post-training for coding models: study Kevin-32B as a verified fine-tune of QwQ-32B with RL claimed, and learn the practical loop of rollouts, reward, and eval.

question: I'm a final-year CS student. I want to really understand LoRA by implementing it myself for my capstone. What should I learn first, what should I build, and which experiments would show I understand it? I have a laptop and one rented GPU for 10 weeks.
plan: Which organisations and teams use LoRA or parameter-efficient fine-tuning in practice, and for what problems (e.g., LLM adaptation, diffusion, domain specialisation)?
Which LoRA variants and related methods (e.g., QLoRA, DoRA, adapters) are used or offered, and how do they relate to each other?
Which tools, libraries and platforms offer LoRA fine-tuning (e.g., PEFT, Hugging Face, cloud GPU services), and what do they support?
Which models were built or fine-tuned with LoRA, and which datasets and benchmarks are used to evaluate them?
Which roles hire for LoRA/PEFT skills, and what do those job postings ask for?
Which benchmarks or evaluation setups are commonly used to compare LoRA against full fine-tuning or other PEFT methods?

notes.finding: LoRA is positioned as a subtype of PEFT and of fine-tuning, so it sits inside the broader parameter-efficient toolkit rather than being a standalone technique.
notes.implication: Learn PEFT fundamentals (adapters, rank, target modules) before LoRA specifics; build the from-scratch LoRA layer as the core artifact.

notes.finding: Hugging Face both offers and uses the PEFT library and trains LoRA adapters on Qwen models (e.g., harness adapters, 3D LoRA fine-tuning); self-claimed via its own blog.
notes.implication: Use Hugging Face peft/transformers as the practical toolchain; replicate a small adapter-training run rather than inventing infrastructure.

notes.finding: Inference/training platforms claim LoRA support: Together AI (Multi-LoRA sharing GPU capacity), Fireworks AI (LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen/Kimi/GLM, merge-into-base inference), Modal, SGLang, CoreWeave Forge; all self-claimed.
notes.implication: Learn adapter-serving and merge-vs-adapter inference tradeoffs; a capstone experiment comparing merged vs runtime-adapter latency would mirror real platform concerns.

notes.finding: Thinking Machines Lab uses LoRA alongside SFT and RL and works on math reasoning; its 'LoRA Without Regret' work reports LoRA can match full fine-tuning when key details are right but lags on high-volume data, and it cites Punica (multi-tenant LoRA serving). Self-claimed.
notes.implication: Design experiments around sample-efficiency and data-volume scaling (LoRA vs full FT) and evaluate on a small math/reasoning set; read both papers before coding.

notes.finding: Most graph-visible LoRA models are diffusion/image adapters (SDXL ControlNet, outpainting, inpaint, LCM-ControlNet, FLUX 3 Image Klein, Photorealistic FX), not LLMs.
notes.implication: A diffusion LoRA (e.g., SDXL style/subject adapter) is a well-trodden, GPU-feasible capstone track and matches where the graph shows real usage.

notes.finding: Other orgs claiming LoRA use span data/labeling and applied AI (Surge AI, LegionEdge, Dharma-AI, XY.AI Labs), suggesting LoRA shows up in domain-specialisation and data-centric pipelines, not only frontier labs; self-claimed.
notes.implication: Frame the capstone around a narrow domain-specialisation task (e.g., domain QA or style adaptation), which is how these orgs appear to apply it.

notes.finding: No role in the graph hires specifically for LoRA/PEFT; adjacent demand is Forward Deployed Engineer (Surge AI, Reflection, OpenRouter), Research Scientists (NVIDIA, Anthropic, Applied Compute) and Software Engineer AI/Agent Platform roles.
notes.implication: Position the capstone as evidence of applied fine-tuning skill (deployable adapter, eval harness) rather than expecting a 'LoRA engineer' job title; target FDE/applied-AI postings.

notes.finding: The graph has no LoRA-vs-full-FT benchmark edges and no QLoRA/DoRA coverage (QLoRA entity exists with zero edges); evaluation evidence is indirect (e.g., AIME'24-style math evals in Thinking Machines' blog). Absence means not covered by the sample, not that it doesn't exist.
notes.implication: Build your own small eval harness (held-out task + a public benchmark subset) and report LoRA vs full FT vs QLoRA yourself; treat vendor claims as self-claimed and note the graph gap in your writeup.

Here's what the graph shows, then my advice.

**What the graph shows**
- **Who uses LoRA:** orgs claiming LoRA use include Hugging Face (trains LoRA adapters on Qwen models, e.g. "harness adapters", 3D LoRA fine-tuning), Together AI (LoRA training incl. Multi-LoRA sharing GPU capacity), Fireworks AI (LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen/Kimi/GLM, merge-into-base inference), Thinking Machines Lab ("LoRA Without Regret" — LoRA matches full FT when key details are right; lags on high-volume data), Modal, SGLang, Surge AI, LegionEdge, Dharma-AI, XY.AI Labs. Tools/platforms: Hugging Face PEFT (offers + uses it), CoreWeave Forge, Tailored Generation, Miles. Models using LoRA are mostly diffusion/image: SDXL ControlNet/outpainting/inpaint LoRAs, sdxl-lcm-lora-controlnet, FLUX 3 Image Klein, Photorealistic FX.
- **Variants/relations:** LoRA ⊂ PEFT ⊂ fine-tuning; QLoRA exists as an entity but has no edges; Multi-LoRA and LoRA adapters exist; "harness adapters" uses LoRA. No DoRA in graph.
- **Roles:** no role hires specifically for LoRA; adjacent demand is Forward Deployed Engineer (Surge AI, Reflection, OpenRouter), Research Scientists (NVIDIA, Anthropic, Applied Compute), Software Engineer AI / Agent Platform, and Fireworks AI hiring across eng/PM/sales.
- **Benchmarks:** no LoRA-vs-full-FT benchmark edges; Thinking Machines used AIME'24-style math evals and SFT/RL comparisons. Most edges are self-claimed (strength 0.5), not independently verified.

**Advice for your capstone (10 weeks, laptop + 1 GPU)**
1. **Learn first:** linear algebra of low-rank updates (ΔW = BA), transformer attention/MLP internals, backprop, then PEFT concepts (LoRA, QLoRA, adapters, rank/alpha/dropout, target modules), quantization basics (bitsandbytes), and Hugging Face `peft` + `transformers` + `trl`. Read the LoRA paper and Thinking Machines' "LoRA Without Regret".
2. **Build:** (a) a from-scratch LoRA layer in PyTorch (inject into nn.Linear, freeze base, train only A/B) — this is the core "I understand it" artifact; (b) then reproduce it with HF PEFT on a small open model (e.g., a Qwen/Llama-class 1–8B) for a narrow domain task; optionally a diffusion LoRA (SDXL) since the graph shows heavy real-world LoRA use there.
3. **Experiments that show understanding:** rank sweep (r=4/8/16/64) vs full fine-tune on a small dataset; LoRA vs QLoRA (memory/throughput/quality); target-module ablation (attention-only vs +MLP); merge vs adapter-at-inference latency; sample-efficiency curve (LoRA vs full FT as data grows — mirrors Thinking Machines' finding that LoRA lags at high data volume); eval on a held-out benchmark (e.g., a small reasoning/math set like AIME-style or MMLU subset) plus qualitative checks.
4. **Scope realistically:** 10 weeks is enough for from-scratch + PEFT reproduction + 3–4 ablations; skip training large models. Note in your writeup that graph evidence is mostly self-claimed vendor blogs — treat claims as directional.

**Caveats:** QLoRA/DoRA/adapters have thin or no graph coverage; no LoRA-specific hiring roles or dedicated benchmarks found — absence here means "not in the sample", not "doesn't exist".

question: I'm a final-year CS student. I want to really understand LoRA by implementing it myself for my capstone. What should I learn first, what should I build, and which experiments would show I understand it? I have a laptop and one rented GPU for 10 weeks.

notes.finding: LoRA is classified in the graph as a subtype of PEFT, and the single supporting source (Thinking Machines blog) calls it 'the leading PEFT method'. Treat PEFT as the umbrella concept to learn first.
notes.implication: Skill to learn: PEFT fundamentals (adapters, prefix/prompt tuning, LoRA) before touching code; build a small comparison of PEFT variants as part of the capstone.

notes.finding: LoRA is also a subtype of fine-tuning, so it sits at the intersection of two well-trodden areas; understanding full fine-tuning first makes LoRA's low-rank trick legible.
notes.implication: Skill to learn: full fine-tuning mechanics (gradients, optimizer states, memory cost) so you can quantify what LoRA saves.

notes.finding: LoRA is one of the most-used methods in the graph (~20 inbound uses_method edges, behind RL 38 and fine-tuning 22, ahead of SFT 17), used by Thinking Machines Lab, Together AI, Surge AI, Hugging Face, Modal, Fireworks AI, SGLang and CoreWeave Forge — all self-claimed, single-source edges.
notes.implication: Project to build: a from-scratch LoRA implementation validated against Hugging Face PEFT (the graph shows HF uses LoRA), since that is the de facto reference stack employers and labs use.

notes.finding: LoRA is heavily used in the image-generation ecosystem (SDXL ControlNet LoRA, SDXL outpainting LoRA, SDXL LCM ControlNet, FLUX 3 Image Klein, Photorealistic FX), all self-claimed single-source edges.

notes.finding: Serving/inference tooling also adopts LoRA (SGLang, CoreWeave Forge, Miles, Tailored Generation, harness adapters), meaning LoRA adapters are deployed as swappable artifacts, not just training tricks — all self-claimed.
notes.implication: Experiment to add: measure adapter merge vs. runtime-swapped adapters (latency/memory), and report adapter size vs. base model — this mirrors how production stacks actually serve LoRA.

notes.finding: QLoRA exists as an entity in the graph but has zero edges, and 'experiments' as a method node has zero edges; the graph simply does not cover them, so no claims about their prevalence can be made from it.
notes.implication: Gap to exploit / caution: QLoRA is a natural extension for a single rented GPU (4-bit base + LoRA), but the graph gives no support either way — verify it from primary sources (papers, HF docs) rather than the graph.

notes.finding: All LoRA edges in the graph are 'claimed' status with one publisher each (mostly the organisations themselves); nothing is corroborated or verified, so treat adoption claims as self-reported marketing-adjacent signals, not independent confirmation.
notes.implication: Skill to learn: source criticism — in your capstone, cite primary papers/docs for LoRA claims and use the graph only for orientation, not as evidence.

Summary of findings:

- LoRA (method:lora) is in the graph as a subtype of PEFT and of fine-tuning (both edges "claimed", single source, Thinking Machines blog quote: "The leading PEFT method is low-rank adaptation, or LoRA"). It has ~20 inbound uses_method edges — among the most-used methods in the graph (top list: RL 38, fine-tuning 22, LoRA 20, SFT 17). Users include Thinking Machines Lab, Together AI, Surge AI, Hugging Face, Modal, Fireworks AI, SGLang, CoreWeave Forge, plus many SDXL/FLUX image LoRA models. All claimed status, mostly self-reported.
- QLoRA exists as an entity (method:qlora) but has no edges — "not in the graph" for its relations; treat as unverified here, though it's a natural extension to study.
- "experiments" (method:experiments) is in the graph with 0 edges — not in the graph as a usable method node.
- Practical advice grounded in this: learn PEFT/fine-tuning fundamentals first (LoRA sits under both), implement LoRA from scratch (low-rank A/B matrices injected into attention projections), then compare against a library implementation (e.g., Hugging Face PEFT, which the graph shows uses LoRA), and try QLoRA-style 4-bit quantization if GPU memory is tight. Experiments that demonstrate understanding: rank ablation (r=4/8/16/64), target-module ablation (q/v vs all linear), LoRA vs full fine-tune vs frozen baseline on a small task, parameter/memory/throughput accounting, and merging adapters. 10-week plan: weeks 1–2 math + transformer refresher, 3–4 from-scratch implementation on a small model, 5–6 experiments/ablations, 7–8 scale to a 7B-class model with QLoRA on the rented GPU, 9–10 write-up. Note the graph is a sample; absence of QLoRA edges isn't evidence it's rare.
